770.heading: Vector Field Map
770.content: A vector field map represents a quantity that has both magnitude and direction at locations across a region, such as wind. Each cell or sample contains two components that can be transformed into speed and orientation. An [[Arrow Plot]] shows local vectors discretely, while a [[Streamline Map]] emphasizes the continuous flow structure. Sampling density and symbol scale must avoid clutter without erasing important variation.

773.title: Vector Addition
773.heading: Vector Addition
773.content:
Vector addition combines corresponding components: $(u+v)_i=u_i+v_i$. In an abstract [[Vector Space]], the operation must be closed, associative, commutative, and possess a [[Zero Vector]] and additive inverses.

Geometrically, addition composes displacements. Algebraically, it combines vectors used in a [[Linear Combination]].

776.title: Varying Cross-Section Bar
776.heading: Varying Cross-Section Bar
776.content:
A varying cross-section bar has an area that changes along its length, so axial stress and stiffness are position dependent. A uniform-bar formula cannot represent the complete member with one constant rigidity.

Finite element treatment approximates the geometry with elements assigned representative areas or uses higher-order interpolation. Refining the subdivision improves the representation of the area and displacement variation.

779.title: Vector Addition and Subtraction
779.heading: Vector Addition and Subtraction
779.content:
Vector addition combines component-wise displacements, while subtraction finds the displacement from one position to another. Adding a velocity-scaled displacement to a position advances an object; subtracting two positions yields the direction and distance between them.

These operations preserve the geometric meaning of their operands only when their coordinate spaces and units agree.

782.title: Variational Finite Element Formulation
782.heading: Variational Finite Element Formulation
782.content:
A variational finite element formulation converts a governing field equation into a scalar functional and seeks nodal values that make the functional stationary or minimal. Electrostatic energy provides a representative functional for Poisson and Laplace problems.

Substituting element shape functions and differentiating with respect to nodal unknowns yields element equations. The approach requires an available extremum principle consistent with the physics and boundary conditions.

784.heading: Document
784.content:

Status: #baby

785.title: Variance Explained
785.heading: Variance Explained
785.content:
Variance explained is the fraction of a centered dataset's total sum of squares attributed to a component or collection of components. For singular-value and principal-component methods, each component's share is its squared singular value divided by the sum of all squared singular values.

Individual and cumulative plots help choose a representation size. A large percentage summarizes dominant variation, but the highest-variance direction is not automatically the scientifically relevant one.

788.title: Variational Induction
788.heading: Variational Induction
788.content:
Variational induction infers causal structure from systematic changes in circumstances and effects. It develops the logic behind the [[Method of Difference]] while allowing evidence to accumulate across imperfect observations and experiments.

A useful method should reason largely from facts, distinguish causal factors from background conditions, and revise confidence as new variations are observed. Its goal is reliable prediction and manipulation, not merely description of repeated correlations.

791.title: Variational Autoencoder
791.heading: Variational Autoencoder
791.content:
A variational autoencoder learns a probabilistic latent representation by encoding each input as a distribution and decoding samples back into data. Its objective balances reconstruction with regularization toward a chosen latent prior.

The regularized space supports smooth interpolation and generation as well as feature extraction. The probabilistic assumptions and tradeoff in the objective influence how much detail and disentanglement the latent variables contain.

794.title: Variable
794.heading: Variable
794.content:
A variable is a symbol, usually a letter, used to represent a number without fixing one numerical value in the expression. It permits [[Mathematical Generality]] because a relationship written with (a) and (b) can apply to every allowed pair rather than requiring a list of examples.

A variable can play different roles. It may denote an arbitrary value in an [[Algebraic Identity]], an input assigned during [[Substitution]], or an [[Unknown Variable]] whose value must be found from an equation. Its written sign does not reveal the sign of its value; (-x) is positive whenever (x) is negative.

797.title: Variable Role
797.heading: Variable Role
797.content:
A variable role records how a column participates in analysis, such as identifier, input, target, risk, or ignored field. Separating role from storage class prevents a numeric identifier from being mistaken for a quantitative predictor.

Role metadata makes model formulas, exclusions, and downstream scoring more systematic.

799.sourceSearchName: variable size temporal point variable size temporal point
799.title: Variable-Size Temporal Point
799.heading: Document

800.sourceSearchName: variable size temporal point variable size temporal point
800.title: Variable-Size Temporal Point
800.heading: Variable-Size Temporal Point
800.content: A variable-size temporal point encodes an additional quantitative variable through symbol area in a time-conditioned scatterplot. Class intervals can reduce a continuous variable to a small set of discriminable sizes, while color identifies groups and position encodes two other variables. Because people judge area imperfectly, the size scale and legend must be explicit. Severe overlap can obscure small points and should be managed through transparency or interaction.

803.title: Variable Name Normalization
803.heading: Variable Name Normalization
803.content:
Variable name normalization converts imported column labels into a consistent, script-friendly convention. Spaces, punctuation, inconsistent case, and unstable prefixes can otherwise make expressions difficult to read and reproduce.

Renaming should be deterministic and documented so the normalized name remains traceable to the original field.

806.title: Variable Subsetting
806.heading: Variable Subsetting
806.content:
Variable subsetting retains only the columns needed for an analysis. The selected set usually includes source variables required to construct the exposure, outcome, potential confounders, missingness flags, and validation checks.

Removing unrelated columns reduces memory use and makes the analytic structure easier to inspect. Selection should be guided by a prespecified research design and documented metadata, since returning later to search the source for variables associated with a desired result can become analytical fishing.

809.title: Variable Elimination
809.heading: Variable Elimination
809.content:
Variable elimination answers a probabilistic query by summing or integrating free variables out of factored distributions in a chosen order. It reuses intermediate results instead of expanding the entire joint distribution.

Elimination order strongly affects the size of those intermediate factors. Conditional independence makes the approach efficient when it prevents many variables from becoming coupled during computation.

812.title: Variable Class
812.heading: Variable Class
812.content:
A variable class describes how statistical software interprets a column, such as numeric, integer, character, factor, or date. The same visible values can behave differently in summaries and models depending on their class.

Class must reflect analytic meaning. A coded category stored as a number may otherwise be treated as continuous, while a date stored as text cannot participate correctly in date arithmetic. Checking and deliberately converting classes prevents these implicit modeling errors.

The book emphasizes deliberate conversion of imported character fields to factors, text dates to date objects, and mislabeled numerics to quantitative values. A class is therefore an analytic decision as well as a storage property.

815.content:
Vannevar Bush proposed the Memex as a personal machine for storing and retrieving a large body of information. It would preserve what people remember poorly while supporting associative trails that match how people connect ideas.

The machine was never built, but its vision influenced later [[Hypertext]] and the World Wide Web. It framed computing as an aid to human thought rather than merely a calculator.

817.title: Vanishing Gradient Problem
817.heading: Document

818.sourceSearchName: vanishing gradient problem vanishing gradient problem
818.title: Vanishing Gradient Problem
818.heading: Vanishing Gradient Problem
818.content:
A gradient vanishes when the error signal becomes very small as it is propagated backward through many neural transformations. Repeated multiplication by small activation derivatives or recurrent weights can leave early layers or early sequence steps with little effective training signal.

Kelleher shows why saturated sigmoid units aggravate this problem and why [[Recurrent Weight Sharing Across Time]] can repeat the same shrinking factor over many steps. Better [[Glorot Weight Initialization|initialization]], rectifying activations, and gated [[Long Short-Term Memory|sequence memory]] are among the responses discussed in the book. The obstacle is practical rather than proof that deep or recurrent networks are impossible to train.

819.sourceSearchName: vanishing gradient problem vanishing gradient problem
819.title: Vanishing Gradient Problem
819.heading: References

821.title: Vanishing Point
821.heading: Vanishing Point
821.content:
A vanishing point is the image location toward which projections of parallel lines in a three-dimensional direction converge. It may lie far outside the visible frame when the lines are nearly parallel to the image plane.

Lines belonging to the same physical direction should yield a common point under perspective projection. Disagreement can expose incompatible geometry in a composite, but inaccurate line selection and nearly parallel image lines make the intersection unstable, so the estimated uncertainty matters.

824.title: Vanishing Line
824.heading: Vanishing Line
824.content:
A vanishing line is the image of a plane's line at infinity. Two distinct vanishing points formed by directions that lie within the same scene plane determine this line and therefore encode the plane's perspective orientation.

The line is useful for checking whether sets of parallel edges belong to a common ground, wall, or object plane. It also supports perspective rectification. As with individual vanishing points, weak or incorrectly identified line evidence can make the estimate unreliable.

827.title: Vanishing Ideal
827.heading: Vanishing Ideal
827.content:
The vanishing ideal I(V) of a subset V of affine space consists of all polynomials that evaluate to zero at every point of V. It is an [[Ideal]] because sums and polynomial multiples of vanishing functions also vanish.

An [[Affine Variety]] is recovered as the common zero set of an ideal. The relationship reverses inclusion: adding equations shrinks the point set, while adding points reduces the collection of polynomials that vanish everywhere.

830.sourceSearchName: value sensitive design value sensitive design
830.title: Value-Sensitive Design
830.heading: Value-Sensitive Design
830.content:
Value-sensitive design is a method for identifying the human values affected by a technology and incorporating them throughout design. It examines direct and indirect stakeholders, investigates how values appear in the context, and connects those findings to technical requirements.

The method helps make apparently neutral design choices discussable, but it faces two limits. Values can conflict, and people may not be able to state all of their practical ethics as explicit rules. It also often assumes the technology will be built. [[Limits of Responsible Innovation]] arise when the ethically important question is whether development should stop.

831.title: Value-Sensitive Design

833.title: Value Stream
833.heading: Value Stream
833.content:
A value stream is the complete sequence through which an idea becomes value delivered to a user. A value-stream map records both active stages and the waiting between them, revealing where elapsed time actually accumulates.

Improving one stage may not improve delivery if another queue dominates [[Lead Time]]. The whole stream, including approval, testing, deployment, and measurement, is the unit of optimization.

836.title: Value Object
836.heading: Value Object
836.content: A value object represents a domain concept defined by its values rather than by a continuing identity. It gives primitive data an explicit type in the [[Ubiquitous Language]], controls how valid instances are created, and can define meaningful operations over those values. A price, title, or user identifier can reject invalid input before it reaches a [[Domain Entity]]. Value objects are preferably immutable, so replacing one value does not create hidden changes elsewhere.

838.sourceSearchName: value object equality value object equality
838.title: Value Object Equality
838.heading: Document

839.sourceSearchName: value object equality value object equality
839.title: Value Object Equality
839.heading: Value Object Equality
839.content: Value object equality compares the constituent values that define a [[Value Object]], not an object reference or independent identity. Two money values with the same amount and currency are equal even when constructed separately. A reusable value base type can enumerate equality components and derive equality and hashing consistently. Every property that participates in the concept's meaning must participate in equality; otherwise collections and comparisons can treat meaningfully different values as interchangeable.

840.title: Value Object Equality

841.title: Validation-Guided Tuning
841.heading: Document

842.sourceSearchName: validation guided tuning validation guided tuning
842.title: Validation-Guided Tuning
842.heading: Validation-Guided Tuning
842.content:
Validation-guided tuning chooses model complexity or settings by comparing performance on data excluded from fitting. The process separates parameter estimation from decisions about the learning procedure.

The selected configuration should then be assessed once on a final test partition that did not influence tuning.

843.sourceSearchName: validation guided tuning validation guided tuning
843.title: Validation-Guided Tuning
843.heading: References

845.title: Validation Dataset
845.heading: Validation Dataset
845.content:
A validation dataset is held apart from parameter fitting and used to compare model choices, thresholds, or hyperparameters. It provides development feedback without consuming the final [[Test Dataset]].

Repeated decisions based on validation results can still overfit that partition, so final performance requires a separate untouched test.

854.title: Valid Argument
854.heading: Valid Argument
854.content:
An argument is valid when its [[Conclusion]] is true in every case where all of its premises are true. Validity concerns the logical form of the inference, not whether the premises happen to be factually true.

A counterexample assignment that makes every [[Premise]] true and the conclusion false proves invalidity. A formal proof establishes validity by deriving the conclusion through a sequence of accepted inference rules such as [[Modus Ponens]].

Vacuum tubes switch or amplify currents through electrons moving inside an evacuated enclosure. Replacing mechanical contacts with electronic motion allowed calculation and logic to operate hundreds of times faster.

Tubes consumed power, generated heat, and failed frequently, making large systems difficult to maintain. Even so, their speed enabled ENIAC, Colossus, and the first generation of electronic computers.

863.title: UV Unwrapping and Seams in Blender
863.heading: UV Unwrapping and Seams in Blender
863.content:
UV unwrapping maps a three-dimensional mesh onto a two-dimensional coordinate layout, like relating a globe to a flat map. Blender's UV Editing workspace places the mesh and its UV coordinates side by side.

Seams tell Blender where the surface may be cut open for flattening. A thoughtful seam layout reduces stretching and produces islands that are easier to paint; pinned control vertices and Live Unwrap can refine the arrangement interactively.

A production-ready layout also avoids unintended overlaps, preserves padding for mipmaps, uses the square texture area efficiently, and keeps island scale proportional to required detail. Hidden or naturally occurring object seams often provide the least visible cut locations.

878.content:
Pinned UV vertices remain fixed while unwrapping or relaxation adjusts surrounding coordinates. They preserve landmarks, borders, or already approved regions while the rest of an island is improved.

Select Overlap identifies coordinates occupying the same texture space, exposing accidental collisions before painting or baking. Deliberate mirrored overlaps can share pixels, but unique lightmaps and independently painted regions require separation and adequate padding.

881.title: Utility Pricing
881.heading: Utility Pricing
881.content:
Utility pricing meters use of a service and charges the consumer according to a defined unit. The payment is usually recurring, and the measured unit may be infrastructure consumption, transactions, allocated access, or another observable quantity.

[[Consumption-Based Pricing]], [[Transaction-Based Pricing]], and [[Subscription-Based Pricing]] are utility-oriented approaches in the book. The chosen unit should follow the value and cost drivers of the service closely enough to be understandable to both parties.

883.title: User-System Loop
883.heading: Document

884.sourceSearchName: user system loop user system loop
884.title: User-System Loop
884.heading: User-System Loop
884.content:
The user-system loop models the flow of information between a person and a computer from a system-centered perspective.

User actions are sensed by [[Input Device]]s. Transfer functions interpret the input as system effects, which update the simulation's data and models. Rendering then turns the updated state into commands for [[Output Device]]s, producing stimuli the user perceives. That perception informs the user's next action, closing the loop.

The model helps locate design problems. Device choice and input mappings affect interpretation, simulation affects the resulting state, and rendering or device [[Latency]] can delay [[Feedback]].

The same structure becomes reciprocal [[Interactivity]] when the user's updated mental state produces a new intention. In games, this cycle forms the [[Core Gameplay Loop]] and couples the [[Game Model]] with the [[Player Mental Model]] inside a larger [[Game-Player System]].

887.sourceSearchName: user developer continuity in blender user developer continuity in blender
887.title: User-Developer Continuity in Blender
887.heading: User-Developer Continuity in Blender
887.content:
Blender narrows the distance between using a tool and programming it. Many interface actions expose Python operators, the scripting workspace sits beside the modeling interface, and the same data can be changed manually or through `bpy` without translation into a separate application.

This continuity supports gradual automation. A user can begin with a repeated manual operation, discover its API call, test it, and grow it into a script or add-on. Development becomes an extension of ordinary Blender work rather than a disconnected software project, although robust distribution still requires explicit architecture and lifecycle management.

890.heading: User-Generated Content
890.content:
User-generated content is digital material created and shared by individual participants rather than only by a platform owner or professional publisher. Social posts, reviews, images, videos, crowdsourced reports, and recommendations can collectively form a major big-data source.

Low publishing friction increases variety and scale, but anonymity, uncertain provenance, and mixed incentives make quality and trust difficult to establish.

893.title: User-Defined Function
893.heading: User-Defined Function
893.content:
A user-defined function adds a custom operation to a data-processing language when its built-in transformations are insufficient. Pig, Hive, and Spark SQL use UDFs to apply specialized record or tuple computations inside a scalable execution plan.

UDFs increase expressiveness and let high-level queries participate in complex algorithms. Their placement still affects serialization, optimization, communication, and reuse across distributed workers.

895.title: User-Centered Design
895.heading: Document

896.sourceSearchName: user centered design user centered design
896.title: User-Centered Design
896.heading: User-Centered Design
896.content:
User-centered design places intended users, their goals, capabilities, and contexts at the center of design decisions.

It begins by understanding the people, tasks, and environment involved rather than treating the technology as the only source of requirements. [[Human Factors]], [[Requirements Analysis]], and [[Task Analysis]] help establish this understanding. Designs are then represented as [[Prototype]]s, examined through [[User Interface Evaluation]], and revised iteratively.

The approach does not imply that every preference becomes a feature. It uses evidence about users to make and evaluate tradeoffs against system goals and constraints.

897.title: User-Centered Design
897.heading: References

898.sourceSearchName: user assessed software quality user assessed software quality
898.title: User-Assessed Software Quality
898.heading: Document

899.sourceSearchName: user assessed software quality user assessed software quality
899.title: User-Assessed Software Quality
899.heading: User-Assessed Software Quality
899.content:
Software quality is partly an assessment made by users, not only a collection of measurable properties in code. A technically efficient and correct product may still be judged poor if it disrupts work, violates expectations, or creates avoidable risks.

This view complements standards for reliability, maintainability, and performance. It asks whether those properties combine into a valuable and satisfying experience in a particular context.

900.title: User-Assessed Software Quality
900.heading: References

902.title: User Timeout
902.heading: User Timeout
902.content:
A user timeout occurs when the assistant receives no expected response within a defined interval. Silence can mean the user did not hear, needs more time, became distracted, or abandoned the interaction.

A [[Dialog Policy]] can reprompt, simplify the question, offer help, or end gracefully. Repeatedly replaying the identical prompt ignores the different reasons that silence can have.

905.title: User Manager
905.heading: User Manager
905.content:
User Manager is the ASP.NET Core Identity service that provides APIs for creating, locating, validating, and updating application users. It coordinates the user store with configured normalization, password, and validation services.

Application code receives it through [[Dependency Injection]]. A seed operation can use User Manager with [[Role Manager]] to establish default users and role membership in a repeatable way.

908.title: User Interface
908.heading: User Interface
908.content:
A user interface is the medium through which a person and a computer communicate. It translates user actions and state into inputs the computer can interpret, and translates computer actions and state into outputs the person can perceive and act upon.

A UI includes more than what appears on a screen. Its components can include [[Input Device]]s, [[Output Device]]s, [[Interaction Technique]]s, widgets, and organizing metaphors. The quality of these components and their relationships contributes to [[Usability]] and the broader [[User Experience]].

In a game, the interface is both a presentation layer and a control system between the real player and the game world. Its [[Game Interaction Model]], [[Camera Model]], visual and audio elements, input devices, and navigation mechanisms jointly determine what the player can perceive and do.

911.title: User Story
911.heading: User Story
911.content:
A user story describes desired value from a user's point of view, commonly as “As a role, I want a goal, so that a reason.” It is a concise placeholder for a conversation, not a complete specification.

The form keeps attention on who benefits and why. [[Acceptance Criteria]] add testable detail when the story approaches implementation, while the Development Team retains freedom to discover the solution.

913.sourceSearchName: user interface evaluation user interface evaluation
913.title: User Interface Evaluation
913.heading: Document

914.sourceSearchName: user interface evaluation user interface evaluation
914.title: User Interface Evaluation
914.heading: User Interface Evaluation
914.content:
User interface evaluation is the analysis, assessment, and testing of a whole interface or one of its components. Its main purpose is to find usability problems so the design can be revised iteratively.

An evaluation method is a particular procedure, such as a [[Cognitive Walkthrough]], [[Heuristic Evaluation]], [[Formative Evaluation]], or [[Summative Evaluation]]. An evaluation approach combines methods in a sequence suited to a project.

Useful evidence includes system performance, user task performance, and subjective response. Speed and accuracy alone do not equal [[Usability]]; learning, comfort, [[Presence]], and other aspects of [[User Experience]] may also matter.

915.title: User Interface Evaluation

The user interface has repeatedly shaped which computing systems succeed. Wartime controls, interactive terminals, graphical workstations, personal computers, search pages, and touch devices all had to fit human perception and action.

Technical capability becomes socially useful only when people can direct and understand it. Interface design is therefore a historical driver alongside faster processors and denser memory.

920.title: User Interface Abstraction
920.heading: User Interface Abstraction
920.content:
User interface abstraction represents an intended interaction independently of one input or output device. A logical selection or manipulation can be bound to tracked props, touch, gesture, or another modality appropriate to the active AR platform.

Separating meaning from device events supports reuse and multimodal alternatives. The binding still needs access to physical context, because an interaction mapped without regard to tracking, feedback, and environment may no longer preserve its intended behavior.

922.title: User Behavior Prediction
922.heading: Document

923.sourceSearchName: user behavior prediction user behavior prediction
923.title: User Behavior Prediction
923.heading: User Behavior Prediction
923.content:
User behavior prediction uses actions such as posting, commenting, sharing, browsing, visiting, or voting to forecast later activity. Because these behaviors change over time, models often represent them as rates or time series.

Early behavior may predict final content attention or behavior outside the platform, such as revenue. The model must account for platform-specific actions and the visibility mechanisms that expose users to content.

925.title: User Experience Evaluation
925.heading: Document

926.sourceSearchName: user experience evaluation user experience evaluation
926.title: User Experience Evaluation
926.heading: User Experience Evaluation
926.content:
User experience evaluation is the process of assessing or measuring aspects of a person's [[User Experience]] with an artifact. It may consider [[Usability]], usefulness, emotional impact, comfort, or qualities specific to an environment, such as [[Presence]].

No single measure captures the whole experience. Evaluators combine evidence such as system metrics, task speed and accuracy, observations, interviews, questionnaires, and physiological measures. The appropriate combination depends on the question, users, task, context, and stage of design.

Evaluation should inform iterative design rather than occur only after implementation is complete.

927.sourceSearchName: user experience evaluation user experience evaluation

928.heading: Document

2026-09-05 13:11

Tags: [[Human-Computer Interaction Foundations]] [[Player Experience Design]] [[Player Experience Layers]]

929.title: User Experience
929.heading: User Experience
929.content:
User experience is a person's entire relationship with an artifact. It includes [[Usability]] and usefulness as well as emotional effects such as enjoyment, frustration, elegance, novelty, engagement, and pride of ownership.

UX extends beyond the visible [[User Interface]] to include the system's social context, the surrounding ecology of tools, and what the user brings to the interaction, such as training, culture, abilities, and emotional state. A functionally complete interface can still produce a poor experience if people are uncomfortable or unwilling to use it.

[[User Experience Evaluation]] assesses selected parts of this relationship rather than reducing the whole experience to one score.

932.heading: User Control of Personal Data
932.content:
User control of personal data is the practical ability to understand, access, correct, object to, or otherwise influence how one's information is processed. Control requires usable mechanisms as well as formal statements of rights.

Big-data inference complicates control because derived attributes may affect a person even when they never supplied those attributes directly. Systems must therefore account for both observed and inferred data.

935.sourceSearchName: user datagram protocol user datagram protocol
935.title: User Datagram Protocol
935.heading: User Datagram Protocol
935.content:
User Datagram Protocol sends discrete datagrams between ports without establishing a connection or guaranteeing delivery, order, or uniqueness. Its small transport overhead and lack of retransmission delay suit rapidly changing real-time state.

A game using UDP must decide which messages need its own sequencing, acknowledgment, duplication handling, or reliability. Losing an obsolete position update may be preferable to delaying newer state behind retransmission.

938.title: Usenet
938.heading: Usenet
938.content:
Usenet began in 1980 as a distributed discussion network among Unix computers. Participating machines exchanged categorized postings without relying on a single central server.

Its newsgroups developed a freewheeling technical and social culture. Connections to the Internet later integrated that community with a broader network.

941.title: Usability
941.heading: Usability
941.content:
Usability is the set of qualities of a system or artifact that affect a person's use of it. Three central qualities are effectiveness, efficiency, and satisfaction.

- Effectiveness concerns whether users achieve their goals completely and accurately.
- Efficiency concerns the time, effort, and other resources required.
- Satisfaction concerns whether the system is comfortable and acceptable to use.

Learnability, retention, error rate, speed, ease of use, and comfort also contribute. Usability is part of [[User Experience]], but it is not the same as usefulness: a system can be easy to use yet provide no function that a person needs.

944.title: Usability Engineering
944.heading: Usability Engineering
944.content:
Usability engineering is an iterative process for creating and refining a [[User Experience]]. A representative lifecycle moves through analysis, design, implementation, and evaluation, with iteration within and between stages.

Analysis identifies users, tasks, context, and requirements. Design turns those findings into interaction concepts. Implementation realizes concepts as [[Prototype]]s or working systems. [[User Interface Evaluation]] tests whether the design meets its goals and supplies evidence for revision.

The process can pursue [[Usability]], usefulness, and emotional impact. Iteration matters because guidelines and designer experience cannot predict every problem before people use the system.

947.heading: URL

URLs give the Web a flat navigational surface across geography and hardware. This convenience creates a discovery problem because location alone does not explain a resource’s quality or relevance.

950.title: Upward Causality
950.heading: Upward Causality
950.content:
Upward causality is the production of a higher-level property by distributed actions and interactions at a lower level. No single part contains or directs the aggregate result.

It is the generative direction of [[Emergence]]: local behaviors form loops, and those loops create the behavior of the whole. [[Downward Causality]] describes the complementary influence of that whole back on its parts.

956.title: Upper Triangular Matrix
956.heading: Upper Triangular Matrix
956.content:
An upper triangular matrix is a [[Square Matrix]] whose entries below the main diagonal are zero. Its determinant is the product of its diagonal entries.

An upper triangular system can be solved by [[Back Substitution]]. In [[LU Decomposition]], the factor $U$ has this form, and [[QR Decomposition]] also produces an upper triangular factor.

959.title: Unsupervised Classification
959.heading: Unsupervised Classification
959.content:
Unsupervised classification discovers groups when class labels and often the number of classes are unknown. The data representation, proximity measure, and clustering algorithm determine the proposed organization.

This contrasts with [[Supervised Classification]], where labeled examples define the classes to be predicted. An unsupervised result still requires validation and domain interpretation because the algorithm's structure is not automatically a meaningful taxonomy.

961.sourceSearchName: unsupervised feature relevance unsupervised feature relevance
961.title: Unsupervised Feature Relevance
961.heading: Document
961.content:
2026-09-14 21:34

Status: #baby

Tags: [[Unsupervised Feature Selection for Clustering]]

962.sourceSearchName: unsupervised feature relevance unsupervised feature relevance
962.title: Unsupervised Feature Relevance
962.heading: Unsupervised Feature Relevance
962.content:
A feature is relevant for unsupervised learning when it helps expose structure in the observations even though no class labels identify the desired groups. Relevance may mean preserving local neighborhoods, separating latent components, or supporting a compact and stable partition.

The difficulty is circular: clusters are used to judge features, while features determine the clusters that can be found. Practical methods therefore state an explicit structural criterion and compare candidate subsets or weights under that criterion.

965.sourceSearchName: updateable game object updateable game object
965.title: Updateable Game Object
965.heading: Updateable Game Object
965.content:
An updateable game object exposes behavior that advances its state during the update phase of the [[Game Loop]]. Its update operation receives game delta time so movement, animation, and other temporal behavior can remain frame-rate independent.

The [[Game World Object Registry]] can iterate only the objects that require updates. An object that is purely visual or static does not need to implement this capability.

966.sourceSearchName: updateable game object updateable game object
966.title: Updateable Game Object

968.title: Unsupervised Learning
968.heading: Unsupervised Learning
968.content:
Unsupervised learning searches for structure in data without being given target labels. It can group similar examples, discover recurring patterns, or learn compact representations that later support another task.

Because no answer key is supplied, the discovered structure is not automatically equivalent to a human concept. The method is nevertheless valuable when unlabeled data are abundant and annotated [[Training Dataset|training datasets]] are scarce.

Clustering illustrates the setup: observations are supplied without correct group assignments, so the algorithm must derive a useful organization from the inputs themselves. This contrasts with [[Supervised Learning]], where desired outputs guide every training example.

Kelleher also describes [[Autoencoder|autoencoders]] as a way to learn a representation by reconstructing inputs without task labels. Such representations can later support a supervised model. The book presents increased interest in these methods partly as a response to the expense of annotating ever larger datasets, not as a guarantee that unlabeled learning always replaces labeled evaluation.

970.title: Unseen Data Test Plan

Tags: [[Data Science Deployment and Renewal]]

971.sourceSearchName: unseen data test plan unseen data test plan
971.title: Unseen Data Test Plan
971.heading: Unseen Data Test Plan
971.content:
A test plan estimates whether a model will generalize beyond the examples used to fit it. The book's golden rule is never to test a model on the same records used for training. A memorized training set, including its noise, can score well without predicting new cases reliably.

A training set fits candidates, a validation set supports comparing them, and a reserved test set estimates the final selected model's unseen-data performance. The test set must not guide algorithm selection or train the final model; otherwise it is no longer an independent check.

972.title: Unseen Data Test Plan

974.sourceSearchName: unnormalized graph laplacian clustering unnormalized graph laplacian clustering
974.title: Unnormalized Graph Laplacian Clustering
974.heading: Unnormalized Graph Laplacian Clustering
974.content:
The unnormalized graph Laplacian is the degree matrix minus the similarity matrix. Its low-valued eigenvectors encode directions in which strongly connected vertices vary together and weakly connected regions can separate.

Spectral clustering embeds vertices using selected eigenvectors and partitions that embedding, often with K-means. The unnormalized form can behave poorly when vertex degrees vary greatly because high- and low-degree regions contribute on different scales.

977.title: Unprojection
977.heading: Unprojection
977.content:
Unprojection maps a screen-space coordinate back through the inverse viewport, projection, and view transformations into three-dimensional space. Unprojecting the same screen point at near and far depth values creates two world-space points.

The line through those points defines a ray from the camera into the scene. [[Object Picking]] tests that ray against collision geometry to determine what the user selected.

983.title: Unknown Variable
983.heading: Unknown Variable
983.content:
An unknown variable is a [[Variable]] whose value is constrained by an equation or inequality and must be determined. In (3x-5=28), (x) is unknown because only particular values make the assertion true.

Solving transforms the relationship into an equivalent form that isolates the unknown. A symbol does not become an unknown merely by appearing in an expression; it may instead stand for an arbitrary parameter or a known quantity. Identifying the role of each symbol prevents a solution process from treating every letter as something to solve simultaneously.

985.sourceSearchName: unknown probability distribution unknown probability distribution
985.title: Unknown Probability Distribution
985.heading: Document

986.sourceSearchName: unknown probability distribution unknown probability distribution
986.title: Unknown Probability Distribution
986.heading: Unknown Probability Distribution
986.content:
An unknown probability distribution marks a place where the model has not specified how plausibility is allocated across a variable's values. If that variable is always known evidence in every intended question, its prior factor may cancel during normalization and need not be supplied.

Otherwise the model must represent the available knowledge with an explicit form, such as a justified uniform distribution or a parameterized family. Calling the distribution unknown does not by itself define an inference.

987.title: Unknown Probability Distribution
987.heading: References

988.title: Unix TCP IP Distribution
988.heading: Document

989.sourceSearchName: unix tcp ip distribution unix tcp ip distribution
989.title: Unix TCP IP Distribution
989.heading: Unix TCP IP Distribution
989.content:
A widely used Unix distribution bundled TCP/IP networking software with the operating system. Programmers could build Internet-connected systems from common tools rather than proprietary network stacks.

This packaging helped TCP/IP become a practical standard in universities and research laboratories. Unix expertise consequently became central to early Internet development.

992.heading: Universal Windows Platform
992.content:
The Universal Windows Platform is an application model for Windows devices that uses a defined API surface, package identity, and capability declarations. Its applications can adapt interfaces across different screen sizes and device families while sharing a common Windows codebase.

Capabilities make access to sensitive device functions explicit, and packaging governs installation and distribution. UWP's constraints distinguish it from classic desktop frameworks even when both use C# and XAML.

The stock-checker and bot projects use UWP clients for Windows tablets and desktop chat. The examples combine XAML, view models, commands, and HTTP or Direct Line wrappers while keeping network and identity behavior outside the visual controls.

995.title: Universal Turing Machine
995.heading: Universal Turing Machine
995.content:
A universal Turing machine interprets an encoded [[Turing Machine]] together with its input and simulates that machine one step at a time. It records the simulated state, tape contents, and head position as data on its own tape.

Universal simulation shows that one fixed machine can perform any computation expressible by a machine description. It also makes self-reference possible, which is central to the proof of the [[Halting Problem]].

1001.title: Universal Quantifier
1001.heading: Universal Quantifier
1001.content:
The universal quantifier ∀ turns an open statement P(x) into the proposition ∀x P(x), which is true exactly when P(a) is true for every entity a in the domain of discourse.

Negating a universal claim produces an existential counterexample: ¬∀x P(x) is [[Logically Equivalent]] to ∃x ¬P(x). The order of mixed quantifiers matters because “one entity works for all” differs from “each entity has some witness.”

1004.title: Universal Machine versus Stored Program
1004.heading: Universal Machine versus Stored Program
1004.content:
A universal machine can simulate any other computer when given that computer’s program. A stored-program machine is one particular organization in which instructions reside in internal memory alongside data.

The concepts are related but not identical. Babbage’s Analytical Engine and ENIAC were intended as universal machines even though their programs were supplied externally rather than stored in memory.

1007.title: Universal Basic Income and Automation
1007.heading: Universal Basic Income and Automation
1007.content:
Universal basic income and automation are linked by the proposal to provide people with a regular income independent of employment when technology reduces the availability or necessity of paid work. The policy could separate basic security from a labor market transformed by AI.

Income alone does not answer every ethical problem. Work can provide meaning, relationships, structure, and recognition, while unpaid care already contributes value without adequate reward. The proposal therefore belongs within a broader discussion of [[Meaningful Work Under Automation]], inequality, public services, and how productivity gains should be distributed.

1010.title: UNIVAC
1010.heading: UNIVAC
1010.content:
UNIVAC was a commercial general-purpose electronic computer developed by J. Presper Eckert and John Mauchly after ENIAC. Its name emphasized universality and automatic operation across scientific, government, and business applications.

Presper Eckert used conservative electrical loads to improve vacuum-tube life, giving the machine notable reliability. Although early sales were modest, UNIVAC demonstrated that electronic computing could become a commercial product.

1013.title: Unit Test
1013.heading: Unit Test
1013.content:
A unit test is a fast automated check of a small piece of software behavior in controlled conditions. It gives developers immediate evidence about local correctness and supports safe refactoring.

Many unit tests form the fast base of a [[Testing Pyramid]], but they cannot prove that assets, systems, platforms, and player-facing behavior work together. Broader integration and playthrough tests supply that evidence.

In a full-stack web application, unit tests can isolate ASP.NET Core controller behavior with [[Moq]] and an [[In-Memory Database Provider]], or isolate Angular components with [[Angular TestBed]], [[Jasmine]], and a [[Test Double]]. [[Arrange-Act-Assert]] keeps setup, execution, and verification distinct.

The web-research chapter emphasizes that test code has a maintenance cost and should prove a useful behavior. Its controller/database example spans multiple components and is therefore described cautiously rather than being labeled a pure single-unit test.

1016.heading: Unit of Work
1016.content: A unit of work tracks changes made during one application operation and commits them together. An Entity Framework database context implements this pattern by tracking attached objects and generating the required statements when save is called. Separating it from the [[Repository Pattern]] lets repositories load or add [[Aggregate]]s while the application controls the commit. The unit of work should respect the aggregate's [[Transaction Boundary]] rather than combining unrelated domain operations merely because one database can do so.

1019.title: Unit Name Qualifiers in Conversion Tables
1019.heading: Unit Name Qualifiers in Conversion Tables
1019.content: A familiar unit name may refer to more than one defined scale, so a conversion table must preserve its qualifier. Pryor's alphabetical catalog distinguishes U.S. and Imperial gallons, U.S. dry and liquid quarts, ordinary and U.S. Survey feet, several British thermal unit definitions, computer and printer picas, and different kinds of year. Choosing a factor from the wrong variant changes the result without producing an obvious dimensional error: both ratios may still cancel correctly. The qualifier is therefore part of the unit, not optional decoration. See [[Unit Conversion Factor]] and [[Volume Unit Scaling]].

1022.title: Unit Conversion Factor
1022.heading: Unit Conversion Factor
1022.content: A conversion factor is a ratio between compatible unit scales. Written with both units, it can be multiplied by a measured value so the starting unit cancels and the desired unit remains. For example, the book uses $0.3048\ \mathrm{m/ft}$ to convert a feet-per-second value into meters per second: the feet cancel, and the seconds are unchanged. The orientation of the ratio matters even when its number is familiar. See [[Reciprocal Conversion Factors]] and [[Physical Quantity as Value and Unit]].
